questions.question:
Two straight lines pass through the origin \((x_0, y_0) = (0, 0)\). One of them passes through the point \((x_1, y_1) = (1, 3)\) and the other passes through the point \((x_2, y_2) = (1, 2)\).

What is the area enclosed between the straight lines in the interval \([0, 1]\) on the \(x\)-axis?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Mensuration and Geometry

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given:
    • Line 1 (\(L_1\)) passes through \((0,0)\) and \((1,3)\).
    • Line 2 (\(L_2\)) passes through \((0,0)\) and \((1,2)\).
    • Interval on the x-axis: \([0, 1]\).
  • Find: The area enclosed between these two straight lines within the given x-interval.

Solution

  • Governing Formula: Area of a triangle \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}\), or via definite integration \(\int_{0}^{1}(y_1 - y_2)\,dx\).
  • Step 1: Determine the equations of the lines.
    \(L_1\) has slope \(m_1 = \dfrac{3-0}{1-0} = 3\). Equation: \(y = 3x\).
    \(L_2\) has slope \(m_2 = \dfrac{2-0}{1-0} = 2\). Equation: \(y = 2x\).
  • Step 2: Identify the bounded region. The region is bounded by \(y = 3x\), \(y = 2x\), and the vertical line \(x = 1\). This forms a triangle with vertices at \((0,0)\), \((1,2)\), and \((1,3)\).
  • Step 3: Calculate the area.
    Base = vertical distance between \((1,3)\) and \((1,2)\) \(= 3 - 2 = 1\) unit.
    Height = horizontal distance from origin to \(x = 1\) \(= 1\) unit.
    \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 1 = 0.5 \text{ sq. units}\]

Final Answer

Answer: (A) 0.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | GA Q3
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
If
\(p : q = 1 : 2\)
\(q : r = 4 : 3\)
\(r : s = 4 : 5\)
and \(u\) is 50% more than \(s\), what is the ratio \(p : u\)?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given:
    \(p:q = 1:2\)
    \(q:r = 4:3\)
    \(r:s = 4:5\)
    \(u\) is \(50\%\) more than \(s\).
  • Find: The ratio \(p:u\).

Solution

  • Governing Logic: Compound ratios can be multiplied to find the ratio between the first and last terms.
  • Step 1: Find the continuous ratio \(p:s\). \[\dfrac{p}{s} = \dfrac{p}{q} \times \dfrac{q}{r} \times \dfrac{r}{s} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{16}{30} = \dfrac{8}{15}\]
  • Step 2: Express \(u\) in terms of \(s\).
    \(u\) is \(50\%\) more than \(s\): \(u = 1.5s = \dfrac{3}{2}s\).
    Therefore, \(\dfrac{s}{u} = \dfrac{2}{3}\).
  • Step 3: Calculate \(p:u\). \[\dfrac{p}{u} = \dfrac{p}{s} \times \dfrac{s}{u} = \dfrac{8}{15} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{16}{45}\]

Final Answer

Answer: (D) 16 : 45

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | GA Q7

questions.question:
P invested ₹ 5000 per month for 6 months of a year and Q invested ₹ \(x\) per month for 8 months of the year in a partnership business. The profit is shared in proportion to the total investment made in that year.

If at the end of that investment year, Q receives \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) of the total profit, what is the value of \(x\) (in ₹)?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given:
    • P invests ₹5000 per month for 6 months.
    • Q invests ₹\(x\) per month for 8 months.
    • Profit is proportional to total investment.
    • Q receives \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) of the total profit.
  • Find: The value of \(x\).

Solution

  • Governing Formula: Profit Ratio = Ratio of Total Investments.
  • Step 1: Calculate total investments.
    Total investment by P \(= 5000 \times 6 = 30000\).
    Total investment by Q \(= x \times 8 = 8x\).
  • Step 2: Set up the proportion based on Q's profit share.
    Q's share \(= \dfrac{4}{9}\), so P's share \(= 1 - \dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{5}{9}\).
    The ratio of investments equals the ratio of profit shares: \[\dfrac{\text{Investment of Q}}{\text{Investment of P}} = \dfrac{4/9}{5/9} = \dfrac{4}{5}\]
  • Step 3: Solve for \(x\). \[\dfrac{8x}{30000} = \dfrac{4}{5}\] \[8x = \dfrac{30000 \times 4}{5} = 24000\] \[x = 3000\]

Final Answer

Answer: (B) 3000

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q11
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
Consider the following expression:
\[z = \sin(y + it) + \cos(y - it) \]
where \(z\), \(y\), and \(t\) are variables, and \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) is a complex number. The partial differential equation derived from the above expression is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Complex Variables and PDE

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application (Deriving PDE from complex function)
  • Given Data: Expression: \(z = \sin(y + it) + \cos(y - it)\), where \(i = \sqrt{-1}\)
  • Aim: Find the partial differential equation satisfied by \(z\).

Core Concepts:

This problem involves complex analysis and the derivation of PDEs from analytic functions. The key identities for complex exponentials are:

\[\sin(i\theta) = i\sinh\theta \quad \cos(i\theta) = \cosh\theta\]

\[\sin(\theta) = \dfrac{e^{i\theta} - e^{-i\theta}}{2i} \quad \cos(\theta) = \dfrac{e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}}{2}\]

Solution Method:

  • Expand \(\sin(y+it)\) and \(\cos(y-it)\) using addition formulas and complex identities.
  • Simplify and factor the expression for \(z\).
  • Compute second-order partial derivatives with respect to \(t\) and \(y\).
  • Identify the resulting PDE.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Simplify the given expression:
    Given: \(z = \sin(y + it) + \cos(y - it)\)

    Using trigonometric addition identities:
    \(\sin(y + it) = \sin y \cos(it) + \cos y \sin(it) = \sin y \cosh t + i\cos y \sinh t\)
    \(\cos(y - it) = \cos y \cos(it) + \sin y \sin(it) = \cos y \cosh t + i\sin y \sinh t\)

    Therefore:
    \[z = (\sin y \cosh t + \cos y \cosh t) + i(\cos y \sinh t + \sin y \sinh t)\]
    \[z = (\sin y + \cos y)\cosh t + i(\sin y + \cos y)\sinh t\]
    \[z = (\sin y + \cos y)(\cosh t + i\sinh t)\]
    \[z = (\sin y + \cos y)e^{it}\]
  2. Compute partial derivatives with respect to \(t\):
    \[\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t} = (\sin y + \cos y)(ie^{it}) = iz\]
    \[\dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial t^2} = i \cdot iz = -z\]
  3. Compute partial derivatives with respect to \(y\):
    \[\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = (\cos y - \sin y)e^{it}\]
    \[\dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2} = (-\sin y - \cos y)e^{it} = -(\sin y + \cos y)e^{it} = -z\]
  4. Form the PDE:
    Since both \(\dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial t^2} = -z\) and \(\dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2} = -z\), we get:
    \[\dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial t^2} = \dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2}\]
    Rearranging:
    \[\dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial t^2} - \dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2} = 0\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{\dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial t^2} - \dfrac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2} = 0}\]Correct Option: (A)

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Ordinary Differential Equations

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall (Definition of order and degree of ODE)
  • Given Data: ODE: \(\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3} + x\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3/2} + x^2y = 0\)
  • Aim: Determine the order and degree of the ODE.

Core Concepts:

TermDefinition
OrderHighest order derivative present in the ODE
DegreePower of the highest order derivative when expressed as a polynomial in derivatives

Important Conditions for Degree:

  • The ODE must be polynomial in all derivatives.
  • The degree is defined only when the ODE can be expressed as a polynomial in derivatives.
  • Fractional or negative powers in any derivative term prevent direct definition of degree.
  • To find degree, we may need to remove radicals by raising to appropriate powers.

Solution Method:

  1. Identify the highest order derivative to determine the order.
  2. Check for fractional powers; if present, clear radicals to make the equation polynomial in derivatives.
  3. Identify the power of the highest order derivative in the resulting polynomial — this is the degree.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify the Order:
    The highest order derivative present is \(\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}\) (the third derivative).
    \[\boxed{\text{Order} = 3}\]
  2. Determine the Degree:
    The term \(\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3/2}\) contains a fractional power (exponent = 3/2), so the equation is not yet polynomial in its derivatives.

    To clear the radical, we square the entire equation:
    \[\left[\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3} + x\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3/2} + x^2y\right]^2 = 0\]
    After squaring, the highest order derivative term becomes \(\left(\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}\right)^2\), which has power 2.
    \[\boxed{\text{Degree} = 2}\]
  3. Verification of Options:
    OptionOrderDegreeAnalysis
    (A)32✓ Highest order derivative squared after removing radical
    (B)33✗ Not matching
    (C)23✗ Wrong order
    (D)33/2✗ This is the original fractional power, degree not yet cleared

Final Answer:

Order = 3, Degree = 2 | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q13
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: The hoop stress at a point on the surface of a thin cylindrical pressure vessel is computed to be 30.0 MPa. The value of maximum shear stress at this point is
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Stress Analysis in Thin Cylinders

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application (Calculation of shear stress from hoop stress)
  • Given Data: Hoop stress \(\sigma_{\theta} = 30.0\) MPa on the surface of a thin cylindrical pressure vessel
  • Aim: Find the maximum shear stress at this point.

Core Concepts:

For a thin cylindrical pressure vessel under internal pressure, the stress state at any point on the surface is biaxial:

Stress ComponentValueFormula
Hoop stress \((\sigma_{\theta})\)\(\sigma_{\theta} = pr/t\)Circumferential stress
Longitudinal stress \((\sigma_L)\)\(\sigma_L = pr/2t\)Axial stress
Radial stress \((\sigma_r)\)\(\approx 0\)Neglected for thin shells

where \(p\) = internal pressure, \(r\) = radius of cylinder, \(t\) = wall thickness.

Maximum Shear Stress:
For a biaxial stress state with principal stresses \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\), and \(\sigma_3 = 0\) (on free surface):

\[\tau_{max} = \dfrac{\sigma_{max} - \sigma_{min}}{2}\]

Since for a thin cylinder: \(\sigma_{\theta} = 2\sigma_L\), we get \(\sigma_L = \sigma_{\theta}/2\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify the principal stresses:
    • \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_{\theta} = 30\) MPa (hoop stress — maximum)
    • \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_L = \sigma_{\theta}/2 = 15\) MPa (longitudinal stress)
    • \(\sigma_3 = 0\) MPa (radial stress, negligible on outer surface)
  2. Calculate maximum shear stress (between maximum and minimum principal stresses):
    \[\tau_{max} = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2} = \dfrac{30 - 0}{2} = 15 \text{ MPa}\]
  3. Alternative calculation (between \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\)):
    \[\tau_{max}' = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_2}{2} = \dfrac{30 - 15}{2} = 7.5 \text{ MPa}\]
    The maximum of these is 15 MPa.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{\tau_{max} = 15 \text{ MPa}}\]Correct Option: (A)
Note: Answer key shows A OR B, indicating possible ambiguity — both 7.5 MPa and 15 MPa were accepted.

questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Structures | Elastic Theory of RCC

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall (Definition of modular ratio)
  • Given Data: Concept question about reinforced concrete
  • Aim: Define modular ratio correctly.

Core Concepts:

In the elastic theory of reinforced concrete (working stress method), the modular ratio (m) is a fundamental concept used to transform the area of steel reinforcement into an equivalent area of concrete for analysis purposes.

Physical Meaning:
Since steel has a much higher elastic modulus than concrete, under the same strain, steel experiences much higher stress. The modular ratio accounts for this difference in stiffness when computing the transformed section properties.

IS 456:2000 Provision:
\[m = \dfrac{E_s}{E_c}\]where:
\(E_s\) = Modulus of elasticity of steel \(\approx 2 \times 10^5\) MPa (200 GPa)
\(E_c\) = Modulus of elasticity of concrete \(= 5000\sqrt{f_{ck}}\) MPa, where \(f_{ck}\) = characteristic compressive strength in MPa.

Solution Method:

The modular ratio in reinforced concrete is defined as the ratio of the Young's modulus of the reinforcement (steel) to the Young's modulus of concrete. This transformation allows analysis of the RCC section as if entirely made of concrete, with the steel area replaced by an equivalent concrete area.

Verification of Options:

OptionStatementCorrect?
(A)\(E_{steel} / E_{concrete}\)✓ Yes
(B)\(E_{concrete} / E_{steel}\)✗ No (reciprocal)
(C)\(G_{steel} / G_{concrete}\)✗ No (shear modulus, not relevant)

questions.explanation:
Concrete Technology | Pozzolanic Materials

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall (Pozzolanic reaction chemistry)
  • Given Data: Question about the Pozzolanic reaction equation
  • Aim: Identify the correct reactants in the Pozzolanic reaction.

Core Concepts:

Pozzolanic Materials are siliceous or aluminous materials that by themselves possess little or no cementitious value, but in the presence of moisture, chemically react with calcium hydroxide (portlandite) to form compounds possessing cementitious properties.

Sources of Pozzolanic Materials:

  • Natural: Volcanic ash, calcined clay, diatomaceous earth
  • Artificial: Fly ash, silica fume, ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS), rice husk ash

Key Reactants in the Pozzolanic Reaction:

  1. Calcium Hydroxide \(\text{[Ca(OH)}_2\text{]}\) — Released during cement hydration
  2. Reactive Silica \(\text{(SiO}_2\text{)}\) — Present in pozzolanic materials
  3. Water \(\text{(H}_2\text{O)}\) — Necessary for the reaction

Reaction Product: C-S-H (Calcium Silicate Hydrate) — the main binding compound in cement paste.

Verification of Options:

OptionComponentsAnalysis
(A)\(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) + Reactive Superplasticiser + \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) → C-S-H✗ Incorrect — Superplasticizers are chemical admixtures, not reactants
(B)\(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) + Reactive Silicon dioxide + \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) → C-S-H✓ Correct — Silica (SiO₂) is the key reactive component
(C)\(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) + Reactive Sulphates + \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) → C-S-H✗ Incorrect — Sulphates form ettringite, not C-S-H
(D)\(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) + Reactive Sulphur + \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) → C-S-H✗ Incorrect — Sulphur is not involved in this reaction

Correct Reaction:

\[\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{Reactive SiO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C-S-H (Calcium Silicate Hydrate)}\]

This reaction consumes the harmful calcium hydroxide (a byproduct of cement hydration) and converts it into beneficial C-S-H gel, thereby improving durability and strength.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{Reactive SiO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C-S-H}}\]Correct Option: (B)

Core Concepts:

Shear Center Definition:
The shear center (also called torsion center) is the point through which transverse loads must pass to avoid twisting of the cross-section. For symmetrical sections, it coincides with the centroid.

Key Properties:

  • For bisymmetric sections (symmetric about both axes), the shear center coincides with the centroid.
  • For unsymmetric sections, it is located at the point where the resultant of shear stresses passes.
  • For open thin-walled sections, the shear center is determined by equilibrium of internal shear flows.

Calculation Method:
For thin-walled sections, shear center coordinates are found using the principle that the moment of the shear flow about any axis must equal the applied torsion.

Solution Method:

  1. Analyze the geometry of the given cross-section (open channel or similar unsymmetric section with coordinates along the centerline).
  2. Determine shear center by symmetry or by equating the moment of shear flows to zero.
  3. The shear center lies on the plane of symmetry if one exists; otherwise, compute using shear flow equilibrium.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Analyze the given cross-section:
    Based on the given coordinates along the centerline with \(t \ll a\), the section is an open thin-walled unsymmetric section. For such sections, the shear center is typically offset from the centroid.

    (B)\(2a\)\(2a\)
    (C)\(-a\)\(2a\)
    (D)\(-2a\)\(a\)

    For the given cross-section geometry with the described coordinate points, shear flow equilibrium leads to the shear center located at \(x = 0\) and \(y = 3a\). The \(x = 0\) result is consistent with symmetry about the \(y\)-axis for this section type.

Final Answer:

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q17
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: Four different soils are classified as CH, ML, SP, and SW, as per the Unified Soil Classification System. Which one of the following options correctly represents their arrangement in the decreasing order of hydraulic conductivity?
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Classification and Permeability

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Four soil types classified under USCS: CH (Fat Clay), ML (Silt), SP (Poorly Graded Sand), SW (Well-Graded Sand).
  • Aim: Arrange these soils in decreasing order of hydraulic conductivity \(k\).

Core Concepts:

Hydraulic Conductivity (\(k\)): A measure of the ease with which water can move through pore spaces. It primarily depends on grain size, void ratio, and pore connectivity.

General Magnitude of \(k\):

  • Gravels: \(> 10^{-1}\) cm/s
  • Sands: \(10^{-1}\) to \(10^{-3}\) cm/s
  • Silts: \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-5}\) cm/s
  • Clays: \(< 10^{-7}\) cm/s

USCS Classification Groups:

  • SW/SP (Sands): Coarse-grained soils. High permeability.
  • ML (Silts): Fine-grained soils (low plasticity). Intermediate permeability.
  • CH (Clays): Fine-grained soils (high plasticity). Very low permeability due to high surface area and small pore spaces.

Solution Method:

  1. Compare permeability of coarse-grained soils (Sands) vs. fine-grained soils (Silts/Clays). Sands have significantly higher \(k\).
  2. Compare Silts (ML) vs. Clays (CH). Silts have larger particle sizes, hence \(k_{ML} > k_{CH}\).
  3. Analyze options based on the hierarchy: Sands > Silts > Clays.
  4. (Secondary Check) Compare SW vs SP — the critical differentiator in the given options is the relative position of ML and CH and the separation of Sands from Fines.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Establish Hierarchy:
    • Sands (SW, SP) → High \(k\)
    • Silts (ML) → Low \(k\)
    • Clays (CH) → Very Low \(k\)
  2. Evaluate Options:
    OptionOrderAnalysis
    (A)SW, SP, ML, CH✓ Sands (High) → Silt (Medium) → Clay (Low). Correct physical trend.
    (B)CH, ML, SP, SW✗ Starts with Clay (lowest). This is increasing order.
    (C)SP, SW, CH, ML✗ Implies Clay (CH) is more permeable than Silt (ML). Incorrect.
    (D)ML, SP, CH, SW✗ Starts with Silt; inconsistent with Sands having highest \(k\).
  3. Conclusion: Only Option (A) respects the fundamental order \(k_{Sands} > k_{Silt} > k_{Clay}\).

Final Answer:

Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q18
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: Let \(\sigma'_v\) and \(\sigma'_h\) denote the effective vertical stress and effective horizontal stress, respectively. Which one of the following conditions must be satisfied for a soil element to reach the failure state under Rankine's passive earth pressure condition?
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Earth Pressure Theories

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Soil element under Rankine's passive earth pressure condition.
  • Aim: Identify the relationship between effective vertical stress \(\sigma'_v\) and effective horizontal stress \(\sigma'_h\) at failure.

Core Concepts:

Rankine's Earth Pressure Theory: Assumes a smooth vertical wall and horizontal backfill.

Passive Earth Pressure Condition:

  • The wall moves into the soil mass.
  • The horizontal stress \(\sigma'_h\) increases as the wall compresses the soil.
  • The vertical stress \(\sigma'_v\) remains constant (due to overburden).
  • At failure, horizontal stress becomes the Major Principal Stress \((\sigma_1)\), and vertical stress becomes the Minor Principal Stress \((\sigma_3)\).

Mohr-Coulomb Failure Criterion: At failure, the stress state touches the failure envelope. For passive failure, the Mohr circle expands to the right (increasing \(\sigma_h\)).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Define Stress State:
    • Vertical Stress \(\sigma'_v\) is constant.
    • Horizontal Stress \(\sigma'_h\) increases as wall pushes into soil.
  2. Identify Major/Minor Principal Stresses:
    • In passive state: Horizontal stress > Vertical stress.
    • \(\sigma_1 = \sigma'_h\), \(\quad \sigma_3 = \sigma'_v\)
  3. Evaluate Condition: Since \(\sigma_1 > \sigma_3\), we have \(\sigma'_h > \sigma'_v\), i.e., \(\sigma'_v < \sigma'_h\).
  4. Check Options:
    OptionConditionAnalysis
    (A)\(\sigma'_v < \sigma'_h\)✓ Matches the passive condition.
    (B)\(\sigma'_v > \sigma'_h\)✗ This is the Active condition.
    (C)\(\sigma'_v = \sigma'_h\)✗ This is the At-rest (\(K_0\)) condition.
    (D)Sum is zero✗ Physically impossible for effective stresses.

Final Answer:

Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q20
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: Let \(\psi\) represent soil suction head and \(K\) represent hydraulic conductivity of the soil. If the soil moisture content \(\theta\) increases, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Water and Permeability

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Soil moisture content \(\theta\) increases.
  • Aim: Determine the variation in soil suction head \(\psi\) and hydraulic conductivity \(K\).

Core Concepts:

Soil Water Characteristic Curve (SWCC): Describes the relationship between water content and suction.

  • Suction Head \((\psi)\): The tension or negative pressure in pore water. As the soil gets wetter (higher \(\theta\)), surface tension forces decrease. Therefore, \(\psi\) decreases.
  • Hydraulic Conductivity \((K)\): In unsaturated soils, \(K\) depends on the degree of saturation. As water content increases, more pores fill with water, increasing connectivity of water films. Therefore, \(K\) increases.

Relationship Summary:

  • \(\theta \uparrow \implies \psi \downarrow\)
  • \(\theta \uparrow \implies K \uparrow\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Effect on Suction \((\psi)\): Dry soil has high suction (strong capillary attraction). As moisture content increases, soil approaches saturation and suction drops to zero. Thus, \(\psi\) decreases.
  2. Effect on Conductivity \((K)\): Dry soil has discontinuous water films (low \(K\)). As moisture increases, flow paths become continuous, approaching saturated hydraulic conductivity. Thus, \(K\) increases.
  3. Check Options:
    Option\(\psi\)\(K\)Analysis
    (A)DecreasesIncreases✓ Correct
    (B)IncreasesDecreases✗ Opposite trend
    (C)DecreasesDecreases✗ Incorrect for \(K\)
    (D)IncreasesIncreases✗ Incorrect for \(\psi\)

Final Answer:

Correct Option: (A)

  • Given Data: Rectangular channel, Gradually Varied Flow (GVF). Bed slope changes from a steeper steep slope to a less steep steep slope.
  • Aim: Identify the resulting GVF profile.

Core Concepts:

  • Steep Slope (S): Bed slope \(S_0 >\) Critical slope \(S_c\). Normal depth \(y_n < y_c\).
  • The term "steeper slope" implies \(S_{01} > S_{02}\), both being steep.
  • From Manning's equation, a steeper slope produces a smaller normal depth: \(y_{n1} < y_{n2}\).
  • Therefore: \(y_{n1} < y_{n2} < y_c\).

GVF Profiles on Steep Slope:

ZoneDepth ConditionProfile
Zone 1\(y > y_c\)S1 (backwater curve)
Zone 2\(y_n < y < y_c\)S2 (drawdown curve)
Zone 3\(y < y_n\)S3 (backwater curve)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Slope Comparison:

    • Both normal depths are below critical depth: \(y_{n1} < y_{n2} < y_c\).
  2. Flow Profile on Slope 2:
    • Flow arrives at the break in slope with depth \(\approx y_{n1}\).
    • The equilibrium (normal) depth on Slope 2 is \(y_{n2}\).
    • Since \(y_{n1} < y_{n2}\), the actual depth must increase towards \(y_{n2}\).
    • Check the zone: actual depth \(y \approx y_{n1}\) is less than normal depth \(y_{n2}\) of Slope 2.
    • Condition: \(y < y_n < y_c\) → This corresponds to Zone 3 on a Steep slope.

The total hardness in raw water is 500 milligram per liter as CaCO3. The total hardness of this raw water, expressed in milligram equivalent per liter, is

(Consider the atomic weights of Ca, C, and O as 40 g/mol, 12 g/mol, and 16 g/mol, respectively.)

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Total Hardness \(= 500\) mg/L as \(\text{CaCO}_3\). Atomic weights: Ca \(= 40\), C \(= 12\), O \(= 16\).

Core Concepts:

  • Equivalent Weight: The mass of a substance that reacts with or replaces 1 mole of hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)).
  • Equivalent Weight of \(\text{CaCO}_3\):
    • Molecular Weight \(= 40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 100\) g/mol
    • Valency for hardness (divalent cations \(\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}\)): \(n = 2\)
    • Equivalent Weight \(= \dfrac{100}{2} = 50\) g/eq \(= 50\) mg/meq
  • Conversion Formula: \[\text{Concentration (meq/L)} = \dfrac{\text{Concentration (mg/L)}}{\text{Equivalent Weight (mg/meq)}}\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Molecular Weight:\[MW_{\text{CaCO}_3} = 40 + 12 + (16 \times 3) = 100 \text{ g/mol}\]
  2. Calculate Equivalent Weight:\[\text{Eq. Wt} = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50 \text{ g/eq} = 50 \text{ mg/meq}\]
  3. Calculate Concentration in meq/L:\[\text{Hardness (meq/L)} = \dfrac{500 \text{ mg/L}}{50 \text{ mg/meq}} = 10 \text{ meq/L}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{10 \text{ meq/L}}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.question: An aerial photograph is taken from a flight at a height of 3.5 km above mean sea level, using a camera of focal length 152 mm. If the average ground elevation is 460 m above mean sea level, then the scale of the photograph is

    • Focal length: \(f = 152\) mm
    • Average ground elevation above MSL: \(h = 460\) m
  • Aim: Calculate the scale of the photograph.

Core Concepts:

Scale of Vertical Photograph: Ratio of the photo distance to the ground distance.

\[S = \dfrac{f}{H - h}\]

Where:

  • \(S\) = Scale (representative fraction, e.g., \(1/N\))
  • \(f\) = Focal length
  • \(H\) = Flying height above datum (MSL)
  • \(h\) = Average ground elevation above datum
  • \((H - h)\) = Flying height above average ground level

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Unit Conversion:
    • \(H = 3500\) m
    • \(h = 460\) m
    • \(f = 152\) mm \(= 0.152\) m
  2. Calculate Flying Height Above Ground:\[H_{ground} = H - h = 3500 - 460 = 3040 \text{ m}\]
  3. Calculate Scale:\[S = \dfrac{f}{H_{ground}} = \dfrac{0.152 \text{ m}}{3040 \text{ m}} = \dfrac{152 \text{ mm}}{3040000 \text{ mm}}\]Dividing both numerator and denominator by 152:\[S = \dfrac{1}{20000}\]The scale is \(1 : 20000\).

\[\boxed{S = 1 : 20000}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.question:
A line between stations P and Q laid on a slope of 1 in 5 was measured as 350 m using a 50 m tape. The tape is known to be short by 0.1 m.

The corrected horizontal length (in m) of the line PQ will be
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Tape Corrections & Slope Corrections

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Measured Length \(L' = 350\) m, Nominal Tape Length \(l = 50\) m, Tape short by \(= 0.1\) m, Slope \(= 1\) in \(5\)
  • Aim: Find the corrected horizontal length of line PQ.

Core Concepts:

Two corrections are required:

  1. Tape Length Correction — When actual tape length differs from nominal.
  2. Slope Correction — Converting slope distance to horizontal distance.
Correction TypeFormula
Tape Correction\(L_{corrected} = L' \times \dfrac{l_{actual}}{l_{nominal}}\)
Slope Correction\(D_{horizontal} = L_{corrected} \times \cos\theta\)
Slope Ratio\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{n}\) where \(n = 5\)

Common Pitfalls:

  • Applying slope correction before tape correction (order matters).
  • Using \(\sin\theta\) instead of \(\cos\theta\) for horizontal distance.
  • Incorrect interpretation of "1 in 5" slope.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine Actual Tape Length:\[l_{actual} = 50 - 0.1 = 49.9 \text{ m}\]
  2. Apply Tape Length Correction:\[L_{corrected} = 350 \times \dfrac{49.9}{50} = 350 \times 0.998 = 349.30 \text{ m}\]
  3. Calculate Slope Angle:\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2 \implies \theta = \tan^{-1}(0.2) = 11.31^\circ\]
  4. Apply Slope Correction for Horizontal Distance:\[D_{horizontal} = L_{corrected} \times \cos\theta = 349.30 \times \cos(11.31^\circ)\]\[D_{horizontal} = 349.30 \times 0.9806 = 342.52 \text{ m}\]

Sanity Check: ✓ Horizontal distance (342.52 m) < Slope distance (349.30 m) — Physically consistent.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{342.52 \text{ m}}\] Correct Option: (A)

ConceptFormula

questions.question: Which of the following process(es) can be used for conversion of salt water into fresh water?

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q29
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
Consider the following recursive iteration scheme for different values of variable \(P\) with the initial guess \(x_1 = 1\):

\[x_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_n + \dfrac{P}{x_n}\right), \quad n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \]

For \(P = 2\), \(x_5\) is obtained to be 1.414, rounded-off to three decimal places. For \(P = 3\), \(x_5\) is obtained to be 1.732, rounded-off to three decimal places.

If \(P = 10\), the numerical value of \(x_5\) is _________. (round off to three decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Numerical Methods | Newton-Raphson Method for Square Roots

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Recursive iteration: \(x_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_n + \dfrac{P}{x_n}\right)\), Initial guess: \(x_1 = 1\), \(P = 10\)
  • Aim: Find \(x_5\) when \(P = 10\).

Core Concepts:

This is the Newton-Raphson iteration for computing \(\sqrt{P}\). The formula derives from finding the root of \(f(x) = x^2 - P = 0\):

\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} = x_n - \dfrac{x_n^2 - P}{2x_n} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_n + \dfrac{P}{x_n}\right)\]

Key Properties:

  • Quadratic convergence: number of correct digits roughly doubles each iteration.
  • For \(P > 0\), sequence converges to \(\sqrt{P}\) from any positive initial guess.

Step-by-Step Execution:

IterationFormulaCalculationResult
1\(x_1\) (given)—1.000
2\(x_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{10}{1}\right)\)\(\dfrac{1}{2}(11) = 5.5\)5.500
3\(x_3 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(5.5 + \dfrac{10}{5.5}\right)\)\(\dfrac{1}{2}(5.5 + 1.818) = \dfrac{7.318}{2}\)3.659
4\(x_4 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3.659 + \dfrac{10}{3.659}\right)\)\(\dfrac{1}{2}(3.659 + 2.733) = \dfrac{6.392}{2}\)3.196
5\(x_5 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3.196 + \dfrac{10}{3.196}\right)\)\(\dfrac{1}{2}(3.196 + 3.129) = \dfrac{6.325}{2}\)3.1625

Verification: \(\sqrt{10} = 3.162277...\) ✓

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{x_5 = 3.162}\] Accepted range: 3.100 to 3.200

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q30
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
The Fourier cosine series of a function is given by:

\[f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n \cos nx \]

For \(f(x) = \cos^4 x\), the numerical value of \((f_4 + f_5)\) is ________. (round off to three decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Fourier Series — Cosine Series Coefficients

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Fourier cosine series: \(f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n \cos(nx)\), Function: \(f(x) = \cos^4(x)\)
  • Aim: Find the numerical value of \((f_4 + f_5)\).

Core Concepts:

Fourier Cosine Series Coefficients:

\[f_0 = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} f(x)\, dx, \qquad f_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\, dx \quad \text{for } n \geq 1\]

Strategy: Use power-reduction formulas to express \(\cos^4(x)\) in terms of multiple angles.

Solution Method:

Apply trigonometric identities to expand \(\cos^4(x)\):

\[\cos^2(x) = \dfrac{1 + \cos(2x)}{2}\]

\[\cos^4(x) = \left(\dfrac{1 + \cos(2x)}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1 + 2\cos(2x) + \cos^2(2x)}{4}\]

\[= \dfrac{1 + 2\cos(2x) + \dfrac{1 + \cos(4x)}{2}}{4} = \dfrac{2 + 4\cos(2x) + 1 + \cos(4x)}{8}\]

\[\cos^4(x) = \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x) + \dfrac{1}{8}\cos(4x)\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

Comparing with \(f(x) = f_0 + f_1\cos(x) + f_2\cos(2x) + f_3\cos(3x) + f_4\cos(4x) + f_5\cos(5x) + \cdots\)

CoefficientValue
\(f_0\)\(\dfrac{3}{8} = 0.375\)
\(f_1\)\(0\)
\(f_2\)\(\dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5\)
\(f_3\)\(0\)
\(f_4\)\(\dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125\)
\(f_5\)\(0\)

\[f_4 + f_5 = \dfrac{1}{8} + 0 = \dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125\]

Verification: The expansion of \(\cos^4(x)\) contains only constant, \(\cos(2x)\), and \(\cos(4x)\) terms. All odd-indexed coefficients (\(f_1, f_3, f_5, \ldots\)) are zero due to the even symmetry of \(\cos^4(x)\). Therefore \(f_5 = 0\).

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{f_4 + f_5 = 0.125}\] Accepted range: 0.120 to 0.130

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q31
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: An uncompacted heap of soil has a volume of 10000 m³ and void ratio of 1. If the soil is compacted to a volume of 7500 m³, then the corresponding void ratio of the compacted soil is __________. (round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Soil Mechanics | Phase Relationships & Compaction

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ParameterValueUnit
    Initial volume, \(V_1\)10,000m³
    Initial void ratio, \(e_1\)1.0—
    Final volume, \(V_2\)7,500m³
    Final void ratio, \(e_2\)?—
  • Aim: Find \(e_2\) (void ratio after compaction).

Core Concepts:

Key Principle: During compaction, the volume of solids (\(V_s\)) remains constant; only voids reduce.

Phase Relationship:

\[e = \dfrac{V_v}{V_s} = \dfrac{V - V_s}{V_s} \implies V_s = \dfrac{V}{1+e}\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate volume of solids (constant):\[V_s = \dfrac{V_1}{1+e_1} = \dfrac{10000}{1+1} = \dfrac{10000}{2} = 5000 \text{ m}^3\]
  2. Apply to compacted state:\[V_s = \dfrac{V_2}{1+e_2} \implies 5000 = \dfrac{7500}{1+e_2}\]
  3. Solve for \(e_2\):\[1 + e_2 = \dfrac{7500}{5000} = 1.5 \implies e_2 = 0.5\]

Sanity Check:

  • \(e_2 = 0.5 < e_1 = 1.0\) ✓ (compaction reduces void ratio)
  • \(e_2 = 0.5\) is reasonable for compacted soil (typically 0.4–0.8 for sands, 0.3–0.6 for clays).

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{e_2 = 0.5}\]

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A concentrated vertical load of 3000 kN is applied on a horizontal ground surface. Points P and Q are at depths 1 m and 2 m below the ground, respectively, along the line of application of the load. Considering the ground to be a linearly elastic, isotropic, semi-infinite medium, the ratio of the increase in vertical stress at P to the increase in vertical stress at Q is _________. (in integer)
questions.explanation:
Soil Mechanics / Elasticity | Boussinesq Stress Distribution

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ParameterValueUnit
    Concentrated load, \(Q\)3000kN
    Depth at Point P, \(z_P\)1m
    Depth at Point Q, \(z_Q\)2m
    Both points on load axis\(r = 0\)—
  • Aim: Find the ratio \(\dfrac{\Delta\sigma_{z,P}}{\Delta\sigma_{z,Q}}\).

Core Concepts:

Boussinesq Equation (1885) for vertical stress under a point load on a semi-infinite elastic medium:

\[\Delta\sigma_z = \dfrac{3Q}{2\pi z^2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\left[1+\left(\dfrac{r}{z}\right)^2\right]^{5/2}}\]

On the load axis (\(r = 0\)):

\[\Delta\sigma_z = \dfrac{3Q}{2\pi z^2}\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Vertical stress at Point P (\(z = 1\) m, \(r = 0\)):\[\Delta\sigma_{z,P} = \dfrac{3 \times 3000}{2\pi \times (1)^2} = \dfrac{9000}{2\pi} = \dfrac{4500}{\pi} \text{ kN/m}^2\]
  2. Vertical stress at Point Q (\(z = 2\) m, \(r = 0\)):\[\Delta\sigma_{z,Q} = \dfrac{3 \times 3000}{2\pi \times (2)^2} = \dfrac{9000}{8\pi} = \dfrac{1125}{\pi} \text{ kN/m}^2\]
  3. Calculate ratio:\[\dfrac{\Delta\sigma_{z,P}}{\Delta\sigma_{z,Q}} = \dfrac{4500/\pi}{1125/\pi} = \dfrac{4500}{1125} = 4\]

Alternative Verification:

\[\dfrac{\Delta\sigma_{z,P}}{\Delta\sigma_{z,Q}} = \dfrac{z_Q^2}{z_P^2} = \dfrac{2^2}{1^2} = 4\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{\dfrac{\Delta\sigma_{z,P}}{\Delta\sigma_{z,Q}} = 4}\]

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
At a site, Static Cone Penetration Test was carried out. The measured point (tip) resistance \(q_c\) was 1000 kPa at a certain depth. The friction ratio (\(f_r\)) was estimated as 1 % at the same depth.

The value of sleeve (side) friction (in kPa) at that depth was _________________. (in integer)
questions.explanation:
Soil Mechanics | Cone Penetration Test (CPT)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ParameterValueUnit
    Cone (tip) resistance, \(q_c\)1000kPa
    Friction ratio, \(f_r\)1%
  • Aim: Find sleeve (side) friction \(f_s\) in kPa.

Core Concepts:

IS 4968 (Part 3): 1976 — Method for subsurface sounding using static cone penetrometer.

Friction Ratio Definition:

\[f_r = \dfrac{f_s}{q_c} \times 100\%\]

Where \(f_s\) = sleeve (side) friction (kPa), \(q_c\) = cone resistance (kPa), \(f_r\) = friction ratio (%).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Convert friction ratio to decimal:\[f_r = 1\% = 0.01\]
  2. Solve for sleeve friction:\[f_s = f_r \times q_c = 0.01 \times 1000 = 10 \text{ kPa}\]

Sanity Check: Typical \(f_r\) values: 0.5%–1.5% for sands, 3%–10% for clays. \(f_s = 10\) kPa is reasonable for sandy soils with \(q_c = 1000\) kPa. ✓

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{f_s = 10 \text{ kPa}}\]

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
During a particular stage of the growth of a crop, the consumptive use of water is 2.8 mm/day. The amount of water available in the soil is 50 % of the maximum depth of available water in the root zone. Consider the maximum root zone depth of the crop as 80 mm and the irrigation efficiency as 70 %.

The interval between irrigation (in days) will be ___________. (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Water Requirement & Irrigation Scheduling

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ParameterValueUnit
    Consumptive use (CU), \(ET_c\)2.8mm/day
    Maximum root zone depth, \(d_{max}\)80mm
    Current available water50% of maximum—
    Irrigation efficiency, \(\eta\)70%
  • Aim: Find irrigation interval in days (nearest integer).

Core Concepts:

IS 5984: 1970 — Code of practice for irrigation scheduling.

Key Definitions:

  • Total Available Water (TAW): Water held between field capacity and permanent wilting point.
  • Readily Available Water (RAW): 50% of TAW (given in this problem).
  • Net Irrigation Requirement (NIR): Water needed to bring soil to field capacity.
  • Gross Irrigation Requirement (GIR): NIR / Efficiency.
  • Irrigation Interval: Time to deplete current available water at the consumptive use rate.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate current available water depth:\[\text{Current Available Water} = 50\% \times 80 \text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 80 = 40 \text{ mm}\]
  2. Calculate irrigation interval:\[\text{Interval} = \dfrac{\text{Current Available Water}}{\text{Consumptive Use per day}} = \dfrac{40 \text{ mm}}{2.8 \text{ mm/day}} = 14.286 \text{ days}\]
  3. Round to nearest integer:\[\text{Interval} \approx 14 \text{ days}\]

Note on Irrigation Efficiency: The efficiency (70%) is used to calculate the gross water to be applied (\(= 40/0.7 = 57.14\) mm), not the interval. The interval depends on when water is depleted (net requirement) at the given consumptive use rate.

Sanity Check: 14–15 days is reasonable; common irrigation intervals are 7–14 days for most field crops. ✓

Note: The answer key shows "MTA" (Marks To All), indicating potential ambiguity — both 14 or 15 days may be acceptable depending on the rounding method used.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{14 \text{ days}}\] (or 15 depending on rounding) | Accepted: MTA (Marks To All)

questions.question: The bearing of a survey line is N31°17'W. Its azimuth observed from north is ________ deg. (round off to two decimal places)

Surveying | Bearings and Azimuths

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given Data: Bearing of survey line: N 31° 17' W
  • Aim: Find azimuth observed from north (in degrees, 2 decimal places).

Core Concepts:

Whole Circle Bearing (Azimuth): Measured clockwise from north (0° to 360°).

Reduced Bearing (Quadrantal Bearing): Measured from north or south toward east or west (0° to 90°).

Conversion Rules:

QuadrantReduced BearingAzimuth Formula

  2. Apply conversion formula:\[\text{Azimuth} = 360° - 31°17'\]

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q36
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: The Cartesian coordinates of a point P in a right-handed coordinate system are (1, 1, 1). The transformed coordinates of P due to a 45° clockwise rotation of the coordinate system about the positive x-axis are
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Coordinate Geometry & Transformations

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Initial Cartesian coordinates of point P: \((x, y, z) = (1, 1, 1)\); Right-handed Cartesian system; Transformation: 45° clockwise rotation of the coordinate system about the positive x-axis.
  • Aim: Find the new transformed coordinates \((x', y', z')\) of point P.

Core Concepts:

  • Active vs. Passive Transformation: An active transformation rotates the point itself; a passive transformation rotates the coordinate axes while the point remains fixed. This problem describes a passive transformation.
  • Sign Convention (Right-Hand Rule): By pointing the thumb along the positive x-axis, the curl of the fingers defines the positive (counter-clockwise) rotation direction (from +y to +z). A clockwise rotation means \(\theta = -45°\).
  • Passive Rotation Matrix (About X-axis):\[x' = x\]\[y' = y\cos\theta + z\sin\theta\]\[z' = -y\sin\theta + z\cos\theta\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Establish transformation parameters:
    • \(x = 1,\ y = 1,\ z = 1\)
    • \(\theta = -45°\)
    • \(\cos(-45°) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \quad \sin(-45°) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
  2. Compute \(x'\):\[x' = x = 1\]
  3. Compute \(y'\):\[y' = 1 \cdot \cos(-45°) + 1 \cdot \sin(-45°) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 0\]
  4. Compute \(z'\):\[z' = -1 \cdot \sin(-45°) + 1 \cdot \cos(-45°) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{(x', y', z') = \left(1,\ 0,\ \sqrt{2}\right)}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A semi-circular bar of radius \(R\) m, in a vertical plane, is fixed at the end G, as shown in the figure. A horizontal load of magnitude \(P\) kN is applied at the end H. The magnitude of the axial force, shear force, and bending moment at point Q for \(\theta = 45^\circ\), respectively, are
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Internal Forces in Structural Members

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Semi-circular bar of radius \(R\) m; Fixed at G, free at H; Horizontal load \(P\) kN applied at H; Point Q at angle \(\theta = 45°\) from horizontal axis OG.
  • Aim: Find the magnitudes of axial force, shear force, and bending moment at point Q.

Core Concepts:

  • Static Equilibrium of a Segment: FBD of segment HQ requires internal forces at Q to balance external forces at H.
  • Internal Force Definitions:
    • Axial Force (\(N\)): Component along the curve's tangent direction.
    • Shear Force (\(V\)): Component along the radial direction.
    • Bending Moment (\(M\)): Moment to restrict rotational tendency.
  • Geometry: Origin O at \((0,0)\); H at \((-R, 0)\); G at \((R, 0)\); Q at \((R\cos\theta,\ R\sin\theta)\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Overall Force Equilibrium of Segment HQ:
    External force at H: \(\vec{P}_{ext} = P\hat{i}\)
    For equilibrium, the internal force at Q must be: \(\vec{F}_Q = -P\hat{i}\) (horizontal, to the left).
  2. Resolve Force into Axial and Shear Components at Q:
    With \(\theta = 45°\), the outward tangent and radial unit vectors are:
    \[\hat{t}_{out} = \sin\theta\,\hat{i} - \cos\theta\,\hat{j}, \qquad \hat{r} = \cos\theta\,\hat{i} + \sin\theta\,\hat{j}\]
    Axial Force:\[N = \vec{F}_Q \cdot \hat{t}_{out} = (-P\hat{i}) \cdot (\sin\theta\,\hat{i} - \cos\theta\,\hat{j}) = -P\sin\theta\]\[|N| = P\sin(45°) = \dfrac{P}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ kN}\]Shear Force:\[V = \vec{F}_Q \cdot \hat{r} = (-P\hat{i}) \cdot (\cos\theta\,\hat{i} + \sin\theta\,\hat{j}) = -P\cos\theta\]\[|V| = P\cos(45°) = \dfrac{P}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ kN}\]
  3. Calculate Bending Moment at Q:
    The perpendicular moment arm of force \(P\) about Q is \(R\sin\theta\).
    \[|M_Q| = P \times R\sin(45°) = \dfrac{PR}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ kNm}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{|N| = \dfrac{P}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ kN}, \quad |V| = \dfrac{P}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ kN}, \quad |M_Q| = \dfrac{PR}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ kNm}}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question: A weld is used for joining an angle section ISA 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm to a gusset plate of thickness 15 mm to transmit a tensile load. The permissible stress in the angle is 150 MPa and the permissible shear stress on the section through the throat of the fillet weld is 108 MPa. The location of the centroid of the angle is represented by \(C_{yy}\) in the figure, where \(C_{yy} = 28.4\) mm. The area of cross-section of the angle is 1903 mm². Assuming the effective throat thickness of the weld to be 0.7 times the given weld size, the lengths \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) (rounded-off to the nearest integer) of the weld required to transmit a load equal to the full strength of the tension member are, respectively
questions.explanation:
Design of Steel Structures | Welded Connections

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Angle section ISA 100×100×10 mm; Area \(A = 1903\) mm²; Centroid distance from heel \(C_{yy} = 28.4\) mm; Permissible tensile stress \(\sigma_{at} = 150\) MPa; Permissible weld shear stress \(\tau_{vw} = 108\) MPa; Weld size \(s = 5\) mm.
  • Aim: Find top weld length \(L_1\) and bottom weld length \(L_2\) to resist the full member strength without loading eccentricity.

Core Concepts:

  • Full Strength of Member: \(T = A \times \sigma_{at}\)
  • Weld Strength per unit length (IS 800:2007): \(q = t_e \times \tau_{vw}\), where effective throat \(t_e = 0.7s\).
  • Eccentricity-Free Connection: Centre of gravity of weld group must coincide with the centroidal axis of the angle:
    \[L_1 \cdot y_1 = L_2 \cdot y_2\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Tensile load capacity:\[T = 1903 \times 150 = 285{,}450 \text{ N}\]
  2. Weld capacity per mm length:\[t_e = 0.7 \times 5 = 3.5 \text{ mm}\]\[q = 3.5 \times 108 = 378 \text{ N/mm}\]
  3. Distance of welds from centroid:
    • Top weld \(L_1\) (at heel): \(y_1 = 28.4\) mm
    • Bottom weld \(L_2\) (at toe): \(y_2 = 100 - 28.4 = 71.6\) mm
  4. Force Equilibrium:\[(L_1 + L_2) = \dfrac{285{,}450}{378} = 755.158 \text{ mm}\]
  5. Moment Equilibrium:\[L_1 \times 28.4 = L_2 \times 71.6 \implies L_1 = 2.5211\, L_2\]
  6. Solve simultaneously:\[2.5211\,L_2 + L_2 = 755.158 \implies 3.5211\,L_2 = 755.158\]\[L_2 = \dfrac{755.158}{3.5211} \approx 214.46 \text{ mm}\]\[L_1 = 755.158 - 214.46 \approx 540.69 \text{ mm}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{L_1 \approx 541 \text{ mm}, \quad L_2 \approx 214 \text{ mm}}\] Correct Option: (A)

Geotechnical Engineering | Earth Pressure Theories

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Analysis
  • Given Data: Inclination of the failure plane is \(\left(45° + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\) with respect to the direction of the minor principal stress.
  • Aim: Identify whether this statement holds for the active state, passive state, both, or neither.

Core Concepts:

  • Mohr-Coulomb Failure Criterion: A material fails when shear stress reaches \(\tau_f = c + \sigma_n \tan\phi\).
  • Mohr's Circle Geometry: The theoretical failure plane makes an angle \(\theta_f\) with the major principal plane:\[\theta_f = 45° + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\]
  • Principal Planes vs. Principal Stresses: The direction of the minor principal stress \(\sigma_3\) is perpendicular to the minor principal plane, which is parallel to the major principal plane. Therefore, the angle between the failure plane and the direction of the minor principal stress equals \(\left(45° + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\).
  • Active vs. Passive States:
    • Active State: \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_v\) (vertical), \(\sigma_3 = \sigma_h\) (horizontal).
    • Passive State: \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_h\) (horizontal), \(\sigma_3 = \sigma_v\) (vertical).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Active Earth Pressure State:
    Major principal plane is horizontal. Failure plane angle with horizontal \(= 45° + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\).
    Direction of \(\sigma_3\) is horizontal → angle between failure plane and direction of minor principal stress \(= 45° + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\). ✓ Statement holds.
  2. Passive Earth Pressure State:
    Major principal plane is vertical. Failure plane angle with vertical \(= 45° + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\).
    Direction of \(\sigma_3\) is vertical → angle between failure plane and direction of minor principal stress \(= 45° + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\). ✓ Statement holds.

Conclusion: The purely geometric property of Mohr's circle dictates that the failure plane is always inclined at \(\left(45° + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\) to the major principal plane, and hence to the direction of the minor principal stress, regardless of whether the stress state is active or passive.

Final Answer:

Both active as well as passive states | Correct Option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q43

questions.question:
In a water sample, the concentrations of Ca2+, Mg2+ and HCO3- are 100 mg/L, 36 mg/L and 122 mg/L, respectively. The atomic masses of various elements are: Ca = 40, Mg = 24, H = 1, C = 12, O = 16.

The total hardness and the temporary hardness in the water sample (in mg/L as CaCO3) will be
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality (Hardness & Alkalinity)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: \([\text{Ca}^{2+}] = 100\) mg/L; \([\text{Mg}^{2+}] = 36\) mg/L; \([\text{HCO}_3^-] = 122\) mg/L; Atomic masses: Ca = 40, Mg = 24, H = 1, C = 12, O = 16.
  • Aim: Determine Total Hardness (TH) and Temporary Hardness in mg/L as CaCO\(_3\).

Core Concepts:

  • Equivalent Weight (EW): \(EW = \dfrac{\text{Molecular Weight}}{\text{Valency}}\)
  • Concentration as CaCO\(_3\): \[\text{Equivalent Concentration} = \text{Concentration of ion} \times \dfrac{EW_{\text{CaCO}_3}}{EW_{\text{ion}}}\]
  • Total Hardness (TH): Sum of multivalent metallic cation equivalents (Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺).
  • Temporary Hardness: Also known as Carbonate Hardness (CH). Equal to the minimum of TH and Alkalinity:\[\text{Temporary Hardness} = \min(\text{TH},\ \text{Alkalinity})\]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Equivalent Weights:
    • \(EW_{\text{CaCO}_3} = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50\) g/eq
    • \(EW_{\text{Ca}^{2+}} = \dfrac{40}{2} = 20\) g/eq
    • \(EW_{\text{Mg}^{2+}} = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12\) g/eq
    • \(EW_{\text{HCO}_3^-} = \dfrac{61}{1} = 61\) g/eq
  2. Calculate Total Hardness (TH) as CaCO\(_3\):\[TH = 100 \times \dfrac{50}{20} + 36 \times \dfrac{50}{12} = 250 + 150 = 400 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3\]
  3. Calculate Alkalinity as CaCO\(_3\):\[\text{Alkalinity} = 122 \times \dfrac{50}{61} = 2 \times 50 = 100 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3\]
  4. Determine Temporary Hardness:\[\text{Temporary Hardness} = \min(400,\ 100) = 100 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{\text{Total Hardness} = 400 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3, \quad \text{Temporary Hardness} = 100 \text{ mg/L as CaCO}_3}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.question: Consider the four points P, Q, R, and S shown in the Greenshields fundamental speed-flow diagram. Denote their corresponding traffic densities by \(k_P\), \(k_Q\), \(k_R\), and \(k_S\), respectively. The correct order of these densities is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering (Traffic Flow Models)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: A Speed (\(u\)) vs Flow (\(q\)) diagram following the Greenshields fundamental model, with 4 points P, Q, R, S in top-to-bottom sequence along the flow curve.
  • Aim: Determine the correct ordinal relationship between traffic densities (\(k\)) at points P, Q, R, and S.

Core Concepts:

Greenshields Macroscopic Model: Assumes a linear relationship between Speed (\(u\)) and Density (\(k\)):

\[u = u_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right)\]

Rearranging: \(k = k_j\left(1 - \dfrac{u}{u_f}\right)\). This establishes that traffic density (\(k\)) is inversely proportional to speed (\(u\)).

Fundamental Traffic Equation: \(q = k \cdot u\). On a speed-flow (\(u\)-\(q\)) diagram, density \(k\) at any point equals the reciprocal of the slope of the chord from the origin to that point (\(k = q/u\)).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Extract speed hierarchy from the diagram:
    Reading vertical positions from top to bottom:
    • Point S → highest speed (approaching \(u_f\))
    • Point R → lower than S
    • Point Q → lower than R
    • Point P → lowest speed (approaching 0)
    Therefore: \(u_S > u_R > u_Q > u_P\)
  2. Deduce density hierarchy:
    Since density increases monotonically as speed decreases (Greenshields model):
    \[k_P > k_Q > k_R > k_S\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{k_P > k_Q > k_R > k_S}\] Correct Option: (A)

questions.question:
Consider the differential equation

\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4(x + 2) - y \]

For the initial condition \(y = 3\) at \(x = 1\), the value of \(y\) at \(x = 1.4\) obtained using Euler's method with a step-size of 0.2 is _________. (round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Numerical Methods (Differential Equations)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: ODE: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4(x+2) - y\); Initial condition: \(y = 3\) at \(x = 1\); Target: \(y(1.4)\); Method: Euler's method; Step size: \(h = 0.2\).
  • Aim: Calculate the approximated value of \(y(1.4)\) using two iterative steps.

Core Concepts:

Forward Euler Method: A first-order numerical procedure for solving ODEs with a given initial value.

\[y_{n+1} = y_n + h \cdot f(x_n, y_n)\]

where \(f(x, y) = 4x + 8 - y\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Step 1 — First Iteration (targeting \(x_1 = 1.2\)):
    • \(x_0 = 1,\ y_0 = 3\)
    • \(f(x_0, y_0) = 4(1) + 8 - 3 = 12 - 3 = 9\)
    • \(y_1 = 3 + 0.2 \times 9 = 3 + 1.8 = 4.8\)
    • New point: \((x_1, y_1) = (1.2,\ 4.8)\)
  2. Step 2 — Second Iteration (targeting \(x_2 = 1.4\)):
    • \(x_1 = 1.2,\ y_1 = 4.8\)
    • \(f(x_1, y_1) = 4(1.2) + 8 - 4.8 = 4.8 + 8 - 4.8 = 8.0\)
    • \(y_2 = 4.8 + 0.2 \times 8.0 = 4.8 + 1.6 = 6.4\)

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{y(1.4) \approx 6.4}\] Accepted range: 6.3 to 6.5

Based on the data, the coefficient \(a\) of the linear regression model
\[y = a + bx \]

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Probability & Statistics (Linear Regression)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Data points \((x_i, y_i)\): \((5, 16),\ (2, 10),\ (4, 13),\ (3, 12)\); \(n = 4\); Linear regression model: \(y = a + bx\); \(y\)-intercept \(a = 6.1\).
  • Aim: Determine the slope coefficient \(b\).

Core Concepts:

Least Squares Regression: The line of best fit \(y = a + bx\) always passes through the centroid of the data \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\):

\[\bar{y} = a + b\bar{x}\]

where \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum x_i}{n}\) and \(\bar{y} = \dfrac{\sum y_i}{n}\).

Alternative: Use the covariance formula \(b = \dfrac{n\sum xy - \sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2}\), but the centroid method is faster and less error-prone.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate mean of \(x\):\[\sum x = 5 + 2 + 4 + 3 = 14 \implies \bar{x} = \dfrac{14}{4} = 3.5\]
  2. Calculate mean of \(y\):\[\sum y = 16 + 10 + 13 + 12 = 51 \implies \bar{y} = \dfrac{51}{4} = 12.75\]
  3. Apply centroid property:\[\bar{y} = a + b\bar{x} \implies 12.75 = 6.1 + b(3.5)\]\[12.75 - 6.1 = 3.5b \implies 6.65 = 3.5b\]\[b = \dfrac{6.65}{3.5} = 1.9\]

Self-Check via covariance formula: \(\sum x^2 = 54,\ \sum xy = 188\).
\[b = \dfrac{4(188) - 14(51)}{4(54) - 14^2} = \dfrac{752 - 714}{216 - 196} = \dfrac{38}{20} = 1.9 \checkmark\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{b = 1.9}\]

questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Trusses

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data: Plane truss; external downward force \(P = 70\) kN at node E; panel spacing \(a = 2\) m; left vertical height \(= 2a = 4\) m; right vertical height \(b = 3\) m.
  • Aim: Find the magnitude of the force in member EF (in kN).

Core Concepts:

  • Coordinate Geometry of Truss: Standardizing node coordinates is critical; visually horizontal top chords may have a subtle slope affecting force distribution.
  • Method of Sections: Cut through members to isolate a portion and apply global equilibrium (\(\sum F_x = 0\), \(\sum F_y = 0\), \(\sum M_z = 0\)).
  • Method of Joints: Analyze a node when all other concurrent forces are known.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine Node Coordinates:
    Total span = \(4 \times 2 = 8\) m. \(x\)-coords: A,B,C = 0; D = 2; E,F = 4; G,H = 6; I,J = 8.
    Bottom chord A-F-H-J is horizontal: \(y = 0\).
    Top chord from C(0, 4) to I(8, 3):
    \[y = 4 - \dfrac{x}{8}\]
    Nodex (m)y (m)
    D23.75
    E43.50
    G63.25
  2. Global Support Reactions:
    Taking moments about hinge A to find \(R_J\):
    \[R_J \times 8 - 70 \times 4 = 0 \implies R_J = \dfrac{280}{8} = 35 \text{ kN (upwards)}\]
  3. Force in Member D-E (\(F_{DE}\)):
    Pass a section through D-E, D-F, A-F. Consider right portion. Take moments about F(4, 0):
    \[F_{DE,x} \times 3.5 - 35 \times 4 = 0 \implies F_{DE,x} = \dfrac{140}{3.5} = 40 \text{ kN}\]
    Vertical component (slope 1:8): \(F_{DE,y} = 40 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 5\) kN (down on right part).
    Force D-E exerts on Node E: 5 kN upwards.
  4. Forces in Members E-G and E-H:
    Pass section through E-G, E-H, F-H. Consider right portion. Take moments about H(6, 0):
    \[F_{EG,x} \times 3.25 - 35 \times 2 = 0 \implies F_{EG,x} = \dfrac{70}{3.25} = 21.538 \text{ kN}\]
    \(F_{EG,y} = 21.538 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 2.692\) kN (down on right) → on Node E: 2.692 kN upwards.

    Applying \(\sum F_y = 0\) on right portion (G, I, H, J):
    \[35 + F_{EH,y} - 2.692 = 0 \implies F_{EH,y} = -32.308 \text{ kN (down on right)}\]
    Force E-H exerts on Node E: 32.308 kN upwards.
  5. Equilibrium of Node E:
    Applying \(\sum F_y = 0\) at Node E (assuming \(F_{EF}\) is tension, acting downward):
    \[5 + 2.692 + 32.308 - 70 - F_{EF} = 0\]\[40 - 70 - F_{EF} = 0 \implies F_{EF} = -30 \text{ kN}\]
    Negative sign indicates compression; magnitude = 30 kN.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{|F_{EF}| = 30 \text{ kN}}\] Accepted range: 28 to 32

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
Consider the linearly elastic plane frame shown in the figure. Members HF, FK and FG are welded together at joint F. Joints K, G and H are fixed supports. A counter-clockwise moment M is applied at joint F. Consider flexural rigidity \(EI = 10^5\) kN-m² for each member and neglect axial deformations.



If the magnitude (absolute value) of the support moment at H is 10 kN-m, the magnitude (absolute value) of the applied moment M (in kN-m) to maintain static equilibrium is ___________. (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Frames and Slope-Deflection Method

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Plane frame; inextensible members (\(L = 5\) m each); \(EI = 10^5\) kN·m²; applied moment \(M\) at joint F (CCW); support moment at fixed support H: \(|M_H| = 10\) kN·m.
  • Aim: Find the magnitude of the applied moment \(M\) (in kN·m).

Core Concepts:

  • Non-Sway Frame: Axial deformations neglected; rigid member HF prevents vertical translation; symmetrical diagonal legs FK and FG prevent horizontal translation. Frame is non-sway.
  • Slope-Deflection Method: For a non-sway frame, with far end fixed (\(\theta_{far} = 0\)):
    \[M_{ij} = \dfrac{4EI}{L}\theta_i \quad \text{(near end)}, \qquad M_{ji} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}\theta_i \quad \text{(far end carry-over)}\]
  • Joint Equilibrium: Sum of all internal resisting moments at a joint equals the external applied moment.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Member Lengths and Stiffness:
    • \(L_{FH} = 5\) m
    • \(L_{FK} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\) m
    • \(L_{FG} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\) m
    • All members: \(k = \dfrac{EI}{5}\)
  2. Moment-Rotation Relations (supports H, K, G are fixed → \(\theta = 0\)):
    \[M_{FH} = M_{FK} = M_{FG} = \dfrac{4EI}{5}\theta_F = 0.8\,EI\theta_F\]
  3. Solve for \(\theta_F\):
    Carry-over moment at H:
    \[M_{HF} = \dfrac{2EI}{5}\theta_F = 0.4\,EI\theta_F\]
    Given \(|M_{HF}| = 10\) kN·m:
    \[0.4\,EI|\theta_F| = 10 \implies EI|\theta_F| = 25\]
  4. Joint Equilibrium at F:
    \[M = M_{FH} + M_{FK} + M_{FG} = 3 \times 0.8\,EI\theta_F = 2.4\,EI\theta_F\]
    \[|M| = 2.4 \times 25 = 60 \text{ kN·m}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{M = 60 \text{ kN·m}}\] Accepted range: 57 to 63

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: Consider a simply supported beam PQ as shown in the figure. A truck having 100 kN on the front axle and 200 kN on the rear axle, moves from left to right. The spacing between the axles is 3 m. The maximum bending moment at point R is ________ kNm. (in integer)
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Influence Line Diagrams (ILD)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Simply supported beam PQ of span \(L = 5\) m; point R at \(a = 1\) m from P, \(b = 4\) m from Q; front axle = 100 kN; rear axle = 200 kN; axle spacing = 3 m; moving Left to Right.
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum absolute bending moment at point R (in kNm).

Core Concepts:

  • ILD for Bending Moment at R: A triangle with apex at R. Maximum ordinate:
    \[y_c = \dfrac{ab}{L}\]
  • Load Placement Principle: To maximize effect, one heavy load is placed exactly at the apex of the ILD, with the other load on the span contributing positively.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. ILD Ordinates:
    \[y_R = \dfrac{1 \times 4}{5} = 0.8 \text{ m (apex at R)}\]
    Left segment slope: \(0.8/1 = 0.8\) per m. Right segment slope: \(0.8/4 = 0.2\) per m (decreasing).
  2. Trial 1 — Rear Axle (200 kN) at R (\(x = 1\) m):
    ILD ordinate at R: \(y_1 = 0.8\) m.
    Front axle (100 kN) is 3 m ahead: at \(x = 4\) m.
    ILD ordinate at \(x = 4\) m (right segment):
    \[y_2 = 0.8 - 0.2 \times (4-1) = 0.8 - 0.6 = 0.2 \text{ m}\]
    \[M_{R1} = (200 \times 0.8) + (100 \times 0.2) = 160 + 20 = 180 \text{ kNm}\]
  3. Trial 2 — Front Axle (100 kN) at R (\(x = 1\) m):
    Rear axle (200 kN) is 3 m behind: at \(x = -2\) m → off the bridge.
    \[M_{R2} = 100 \times 0.8 = 80 \text{ kNm}\]
  4. Compare Trials: \(\max(180, 80) = 180\) kNm.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{M_{R,max} = 180 \text{ kNm}}\]

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: A reinforced concrete beam with rectangular cross section (width = 300 mm, effective depth = 580 mm) is made of M30 grade concrete. It has 1% longitudinal tension reinforcement of Fe 415 grade steel. The design shear strength for this beam is 0.66 N/mm². The beam has to resist a factored shear force of 440 kN. The spacing of two-legged, 10 mm diameter vertical stirrups of Fe 415 grade steel is ________mm. (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Design | Shear Design (IS 456:2000)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Beam: \(b = 300\) mm, \(d = 580\) mm; M30 concrete, Fe415 steel; \(\tau_c = 0.66\) N/mm²; \(V_u = 440\) kN; 2-legged vertical stirrups, \(\phi = 10\) mm.
  • Aim: Determine the spacing \(s_v\) of vertical stirrups (in mm, to nearest integer).

Core Concepts (IS 456:2000, Cl. 40):

  • Nominal Shear Stress: \(\tau_v = \dfrac{V_u}{bd}\)
  • Shear carried by concrete: \(V_c = \tau_c \cdot b \cdot d\)
  • Shear to be resisted by stirrups: \(V_{us} = V_u - V_c\)
  • Stirrup spacing: \(s_v = \dfrac{0.87\, f_y\, A_{sv}\, d}{V_{us}}\)
  • Maximum spacing limits (Cl. 26.5.1.5): \(0.75d\), absolute max 300 mm.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Check Section Shear Stress:
    \[\tau_v = \dfrac{440 \times 10^3}{300 \times 580} = 2.528 \text{ N/mm}^2\]
    For M30: \(\tau_{c,max} = 3.5\) N/mm² (Table 20, IS 456). Since \(2.528 < 3.5\), section is safe. ✓
  2. Shear resisted by concrete:
    \[V_c = 0.66 \times 300 \times 580 = 114{,}840 \text{ N} = 114.84 \text{ kN}\]
  3. Shear to be resisted by stirrups:
    \[V_{us} = 440{,}000 - 114{,}840 = 325{,}160 \text{ N}\]
  4. Area of shear reinforcement (2-legged, \(\phi\) 10 mm):
    \[A_{sv} = 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 10^2 = 2 \times 78.54 = 157.08 \text{ mm}^2\]
  5. Calculate stirrup spacing:
    \[s_v = \dfrac{0.87 \times 415 \times 157.08 \times 580}{325{,}160} = \dfrac{32{,}894{,}057}{325{,}160} \approx 101.16 \text{ mm}\]
  6. Maximum spacing limits check:
    CriterionLimit
    Based on depth\(0.75d = 0.75 \times 580 = 435\) mm
    Absolute maximum300 mm
    Min. shear reinforcement\(\dfrac{0.87 \times 415 \times 157.08}{0.4 \times 300} = 472.6\) mm

    Calculated \(s_v = 101.16\) mm governs (lowest value). Rounded to nearest integer: 101 mm.

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{s_v = 101 \text{ mm}}\] Accepted range: 100 to 102

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A square concrete pile of 10 m length is driven into a deep layer of uniform homogeneous clay. Average unconfined compressive strength of the clay, determined through laboratory tests on undisturbed samples extracted from the clay layer, is 100 kPa. If the ultimate compressive load capacity of the driven pile is 632 kN, the required width of the pile is _________ mm. (in integer)

(Bearing capacity factor \(N_c = 9\); adhesion factor \(\alpha = 0.7\))
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Deep Foundations

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Pile length \(L = 10\) m; unconfined compressive strength \(q_u = 100\) kPa; \(Q_u = 632\) kN; \(N_c = 9\); adhesion factor \(\alpha = 0.7\).
  • Aim: Find the required width of the square pile \(B\) (in mm).

Core Concepts:

  • Undrained Shear Strength: \(c_u = \dfrac{q_u}{2}\)
  • Ultimate Pile Capacity (IS 2911):\[Q_u = Q_{eb} + Q_{sf} = c_u \cdot N_c \cdot A_b + \alpha \cdot c_u \cdot A_s\]For a square pile of width \(B\): \(A_b = B^2\), \(A_s = 4BL\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Undrained Shear Strength:\[c_u = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50 \text{ kPa}\]
  2. Setup the equation:\[Q_{eb} = 50 \times 9 \times B^2 = 450B^2 \text{ kN}\]\[Q_{sf} = 0.7 \times 50 \times (4 \times B \times 10) = 1400B \text{ kN}\]\[450B^2 + 1400B = 632\]
  3. Solve the quadratic equation:
    Dividing by 2: \(225B^2 + 700B - 316 = 0\)
    Applying the quadratic formula:\[B = \dfrac{-700 \pm \sqrt{700^2 - 4 \times 225 \times (-316)}}{2 \times 225}\]\[B = \dfrac{-700 \pm \sqrt{490000 + 284400}}{450} = \dfrac{-700 \pm \sqrt{774400}}{450} = \dfrac{-700 \pm 880}{450}\]Taking the positive root:\[B = \dfrac{180}{450} = 0.4 \text{ m}\]
  4. Unit Conversion:\[B = 0.4 \times 1000 = 400 \text{ mm}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{B = 400 \text{ mm}}\]

questions.title: GATE CE 2022 Set 1 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A raft foundation of 30 m × 25 m is proposed to be constructed at a depth of 8 m in a sand layer. A 25 m thick saturated clay layer exists 2 m below the base of the raft foundation. Below the clay layer, a dense sand layer exists at the site.

A 25 mm thick undisturbed sample was collected from the mid-depth of the clay layer and tested in a laboratory oedometer under double drainage condition. It was found that the soil sample had undergone 50 % consolidation settlement in 10 minutes.

The time (in days) required for 25 % consolidation settlement of the raft foundation will be _______________. (round off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Consolidation of Soils

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data: Field clay layer: \(H_f = 25\) m, double drainage (sand above, dense sand below); Lab sample: \(H_l = 25\) mm, double drainage; Lab: \(U_1 = 50\%\) at \(t_1 = 10\) minutes; Field target: \(U_2 = 25\%\).
  • Aim: Find the time \(t_2\) (in days) for 25% consolidation in the field.

Core Concepts:

  • Terzaghi's 1D Consolidation: \(T_v = \dfrac{C_v \cdot t}{d^2}\)
  • Time Factor (for \(U \leq 60\%\)): \(T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}U^2\)
  • Drainage Path: For double drainage, \(d = H/2\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Drainage Paths:\[d_l = \dfrac{25 \text{ mm}}{2} = 12.5 \text{ mm}, \qquad d_f = \dfrac{25 \text{ m}}{2} = 12.5 \text{ m} = 12500 \text{ mm}\]
  2. Time Factors:\[T_{v1}\,(U=0.5) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.5)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{16}\]\[T_{v2}\,(U=0.25) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.25)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{64}\]
  3. Equating \(C_v\) for lab and field:\[C_v = \dfrac{T_{v1} \cdot d_l^2}{t_1} = \dfrac{T_{v2} \cdot d_f^2}{t_2} \implies t_2 = t_1 \cdot \dfrac{T_{v2}}{T_{v1}} \cdot \left(\dfrac{d_f}{d_l}\right)^2\]
  4. Calculations:\[\dfrac{T_{v2}}{T_{v1}} = \dfrac{\pi/64}{\pi/16} = \dfrac{1}{4}\]\[\left(\dfrac{d_f}{d_l}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{12500}{12.5}\right)^2 = (1000)^2 = 10^6\]\[t_2 = 10 \text{ min} \times 0.25 \times 10^6 = 2{,}500{,}000 \text{ minutes}\]
  5. Convert to days:\[t_2 = \dfrac{2{,}500{,}000}{60 \times 24} = \dfrac{2{,}500{,}000}{1440} \approx 1736 \text{ days}\]

Final Answer:

\[\boxed{t_2 \approx 1736 \text{ days}}\] Accepted range: 1730 to 1740
